Course: Algorithms (week 4, topic: binary search preconditions, status: KNOWN).

Question: explain binary search preconditions to someone who has just got it wrong. This is for Algorithms week 4. Tell me what is missing before I submit it.

Student answer: Hash tables give O(1) lookup.

Official rubric points:
1. States the sortedness precondition
2. Says each step halves the remaining range
3. Says sorting first costs more than one linear scan
4. Mentions a correct mid or termination detail

Verdict: incorrect. None of the 4 points are covered, and the reason is one wrong assumption doing all the damage.

Not earned: all 4 points. Your answer says "Hash tables give O(1) lookup." - and none of the rubric points can be read into that.

What is actually going wrong: treating binary search as a faster search rather than as an algorithm that buys speed with a precondition someone has to pay for.
The correction: Check the precondition before choosing the algorithm, and amortise the sort over the number of searches you will actually do.
Why it works that way: Halving is only valid if one comparison tells you which half to discard, and that inference is what sortedness provides.

To prove the fix stuck: Count the searches your program performs per load of the data, then decide between one sort plus many binary searches and repeated linear scans, with the arithmetic written out.

- Point 2: Says an IP address is used for routing between networks
- Point 4: Names ARP or its role

The misconception underneath this: that the two addresses are alternative names for the same machine, rather than addresses that operate at different scopes.
The correction: Attach each address to its scope: the MAC gets the frame across one link, the IP gets the packet across the internet, and the MAC pair is rewritten at every hop.
Why: Routers make forwarding decisions on the network layer address because MAC addresses carry no location information - they cannot be aggregated into routes.

Official rubric points:

3. Says inner objects are still shared after a shallow copy
4. Names the deep copy when independence is required

Not earned: all 4 points. Your answer says "I copied the grid with a slice, so changing the copy cannot affect the original. The shared rows must be a bug elsewhere." - and none of the rubric points can be read into that.

The idea that needs replacing: that copying is a single operation with one meaning, when it has a depth and the default depth is one level.
The fix, concretely: Copy to the depth your program needs: a slice duplicates the outer list only, so nested rows stay shared until you deep copy.
Why it works that way: A shallow copy duplicates the container and re-uses the references inside it, so mutating an inner object is visible through both containers.

Question: Practice question for Data Structures: describe heaps and priority queues and justify the choice you would make. I want the honest grading, not encouragement.

Student answer: A priority queue keeps the list sorted at all times, so every insert costs O(n log n) to re-sort.

Official rubric points:
1. Says a heap keeps the extreme element at the root
2. Says a heap is partially ordered, not sorted
3. Gives the costs of insert and extract
4. Says peeking at the extreme is constant time

Verdict: incorrect. None of the 4 points are covered, and the reason is one wrong assumption doing all the damage.

Not earned: all 4 points. Your answer says "A priority queue keeps the list sorted at all times, so every insert costs O(n log n) to re-sort." - and none of the rubric points can be read into that.

The misconception underneath this: that a priority queue must keep everything sorted, so maintaining it costs as much as sorting.
The correct statement: Use a heap: it maintains only the parent-child ordering you need, so inserts and extractions are logarithmic rather than full re-sorts.
The mechanism: Keeping a total order is more work than any single query needs; the heap invariant is the weakest ordering that still guarantees the top element.

To prove the fix stuck: Insert 1,000 random values into a sorted list and into a heap, timing both, then extract the minimum 1,000 times and compare again.

I think this API is broken. My code:

```js
let data;
fetch('/api/courses')
  .then(res => res.json())
  .then(json => { data = json; });
console.log(data); // undefined!!
```

I can literally SEE the request succeed with a 200 in the network tab, and `data = json` definitely runs because a log inside there prints the courses. But the outer console.log prints undefined. How is that possible if the request works?

The API is innocent — and your two observations ('the inner log prints data' but 'the outer log prints undefined') are actually the complete evidence. They just happen in a different ORDER than the source code reads.

Do this: put `console.log('A')` inside your second `.then`, and `console.log('B')` on the outer console.log line. Run it. Which letter prints first?
B prints first?! But B is written BELOW the fetch. How does JavaScript run my code out of order?

It doesn't run out of order — it runs in two waves, and that's the mental model shift.

Wave 1: JavaScript executes your script top to bottom WITHOUT stopping. `fetch(...)` doesn't perform the download right there — it only *starts* it and registers your `.then` callbacks as 'call these later, when the response lands.' Then it keeps going and runs your outer `console.log(data)` — at which point `data` was never assigned. That's B.

Wave 2: milliseconds later the response arrives, and only now do your `.then` callbacks run. That's A, and that's when `data` finally gets its value — too late for B.
Inside the .then chain... or somewhere that runs during Wave 2. So I should move my rendering code into the .then instead of trying to smuggle data out into a global variable?

Exactly — 'smuggling data out to the top level' is the anti-pattern, and you named it yourself. Code that depends on the response belongs downstream of the response: inside the `.then`, or in a function the `.then` calls.

Restructure it that way and run it. Then, one more experiment so this generalizes: wrap the same logic in an `async` function using `await fetch(...)` and log your A/B letters again. You'll see `await` doesn't break the two-wave model — it's syntax that lets you write Wave 2 code so it *reads* like Wave 1. Tell me what order you get.

I've spent three days hunting a duplicate-rows bug that doesn't exist. Users swear items show up at the bottom of page 1 AND the top of page 2, and other items never show up at all. But I've queried the table directly — no duplicate rows, no missing rows, data is perfect! My endpoint is just SELECT * FROM activities ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 20 OFFSET 20*(page-1). The data is clean, the query is textbook... is the driver duplicating rows in transit?

Your data is clean and your query is textbook — and both facts survive while the users are ALSO right. Here's the reframe that dissolves the paradox: the users aren't making one query; they're making a SEQUENCE of queries with time gaps between them, against a table that's alive. Simulate it by hand with a 5-row table, page size 2, newest first.

Page 1: newest two — E, D. Then F inserts at the top, so the order is now F E D C B A. Page 2 says 'skip 2, take 2': skips F and E... returns D, C. D AGAIN — the user just saw D at the bottom of page 1! The insert shifted every existing row down one position, so the skip-counter skips F (never seen) and E (seen), and re-serves D. And it's worse in the other direction: if rows got DELETED between clicks, everything shifts UP and the skip-counter would jump OVER a row the user never saw. Duplicates from inserts, gaps from deletes — and my feed has constant inserts. There is no bug in the data. OFFSET is counting from a moving edge.

'Counting from a moving edge' — that's the whole disease in five words. OFFSET doesn't identify rows; it counts positions from the top, and the top of a newest-first live feed is precisely the most unstable location in the entire table. So: design the cure. The user's real request isn't 'rows at positions 21-40' — nobody thinks in positions.

'Show me what comes AFTER the last thing I saw.' The anchor should be the CONTENT, not the position — the query should be WHERE created_at < [D's timestamp] ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 20. Then new inserts at the top can't shift anything: D's timestamp is a fixed point, and 'older than D' is stable no matter what arrives above. The API returns each page plus a cursor — the last row's timestamp — and the client sends it back for the next page. Wait, one hole: what if two activities share the exact same timestamp? The boundary would be ambiguous — I could still skip or duplicate WITHIN a timestamp tie.

Catching the tie-break hole yourself puts you ahead of half the production implementations out there. The standard fix: a compound cursor — ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC with WHERE (created_at, id) < (:ts, :id). The id disambiguates ties, and since it's unique, every boundary is exact.

My toolchain is broken — third gcc reinstall and STILL: 'undefined reference to matrix_multiply'. The function is RIGHT THERE: declared in matrix.h, which I include, and main.c compiles with zero errors. It even says the error comes from something called 'ld', not gcc. The install must be corrupt somewhere.

That 'ld' in the message is the whole story — you're being rejected by a different program than the one you've been reinstalling. Look at the evidence sequence: main.c COMPILED cleanly, then something named ld complained. Two programs, two stages, two different questions being asked. Here's stage one's question: when the compiler saw `matrix_multiply(a, b)` in main.c, knowing only what matrix.h told it — what could it actually CHECK, and what did it have to take on faith?

The header only has the signature — `Matrix matrix_multiply(Matrix a, Matrix b);` — so the compiler could check I'm calling it with the right types and using the return value correctly. But the actual BODY of the function... the header never contains that. So the compiler took on faith that the body exists somewhere else? A declaration is like a... promise? 'This function exists, someone will provide it.'

Exactly: declaration is a promise, definition is the delivery — and the linker (ld) is the stage that collects deliveries. The compiler turns each .c file into a .o file with IOUs in it: 'I call matrix_multiply, address to be filled in later.' The linker's job is matching every IOU to a definition across all the .o files you hand it. So now diagnose yourself: your compile command is `gcc main.c -o program`. Where was matrix_multiply's DEFINITION supposed to come from, and did you ever hand it to the linker?

The definition is in matrix.c... which I never mentioned in the command! I only ever compiled main.c. Including matrix.h just pasted the promises into main.c — it never pulled in matrix.c. So the linker collected one .o full of IOUs and had no delivery to match. `gcc main.c matrix.c -o program` should fix it... but wait, why is it even split like this? Why doesn't the compiler just go FIND matrix.c itself — it's right there in the same folder!

Because the split is a feature you'll be grateful for by your third big project: separate compilation means each .c becomes a .o INDEPENDENTLY — change one file in a million-line project and you recompile one file, then re-link, instead of recompiling the world. It's also how libraries work: printf's definition isn't in any .c you own — it arrives as a precompiled library the linker matches your IOU against.
